Both $k$ and $K$ are real and positive, so the right side is real; the channel factor $S_{0}=e^{2i\delta_{0}}$ has modulus one by [[pthm-nrqm-scattering-partial-wave-cross-section]] clause (b).

Let $E\to0^{+}$, so $k\to0$ and $K\to K_{0}:=\sqrt{2mU}/\hbar$. Since $(k/K)\tan(Ka)\to0$, the first term is $\arctan\bigl((k/K)\tan(Ka)\bigr)=k\tan(K_{0}a)/K_{0}+O(k^{3})$, hence $\delta_{0}(k)=-k\,a_{\mathrm{eff}}+O(k^{3})$ with $a_{\mathrm{eff}}:=a-\tan(K_{0}a)/K_{0}$, and the s-wave channel reading of [[pthm-nrqm-scattering-partial-wave-cross-section]] clause (b) is $\sigma_{0}=4\pi\sin^{2}\delta_{0}/k^{2}\to4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}$.

The low-energy behaviour separates two depth regimes. If $K_{0}a\to(n+\frac12)\pi$ from below, then $\tan(K_{0}a)\to+\infty$ and $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to-\infty$, so the low-energy $s$-wave cross-section reading $4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}$ diverges: this is the zero-energy resonance of the well at which a new bound state appears, not a hard-sphere limit. If instead $\tan(K_{0}a)/K_{0}\to0$, then $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to a$ and $\sigma_{0}\to4\pi a^{2}$, the low-energy $s$-wave reading of a hard sphere of radius $a$, four times its geometric cross section $\pi a^{2}$; at the depths $K_{0}a=n\pi$ of this class one has $\tan(K_{0}a)=0$ exactly, hence $a_{\mathrm{eff}}=a$ and $\delta_{0}(k)=-ka+O(k^{3})$, and the interior regular solution has a node approaching $r=a$, which is the vanishing boundary condition of the hard sphere.

As a consistency check of the matching algebra, set $U=0$; then $K=k$ and the relation $K\cot(Ka)=k\cot(ka+\delta_{0})$ gives $\delta_{0}=0$ modulo $\pi$, which is the correct free case; and at an energy with $\tan(Ka)=0$, i.e. $Ka=n\pi$, the matching gives $k\cot(ka+\delta_{0})=K\cot(Ka)\to\infty$, i.e. $\sin(ka+\delta_{0})=0$, so $\delta_{0}=-ka$ modulo $\pi$: at such an energy the interior solution vanishes at $r=a$ and the exterior phase is that of a hard sphere of radius $a$.

after.claim: For $r<a$ the reduced equation is $u_0''=-K^2u_0$, so its nonzero real regular solution is $u_0(r)=A\sin(Kr)$, $A\ne0$, with $u_0(0)=0$; the normalization in [F1] corresponds to $A=1/K$. For $r>a$ a nonzero real solution has the form $B\sin(kr+\delta_0)$ with real $B\ne0$. The regular solution and its derivative are absolutely continuous locally through the bounded step potential; integrating the radial equation across $a$ gives no jump of $u_0'$ or $u_0$. Thus $A\sin(Ka)=B\sin(ka+\delta_0)$ and $AK\cos(Ka)=Bk\cos(ka+\delta_0)$.

Put $X:=K\cos(Ka)$, $Y:=k\sin(Ka)$ and $z:=X+iY$. Since $k,K>0$ and sine and cosine cannot both vanish, $X^2+Y^2>0$. With $\theta:=ka+\delta_0$, the matching equations give $Bk\cos\theta=AX$, $Bk\sin\theta=AY$, hence $e^{2i\theta}=z/\overline z$ regardless of the real sign of $A/B$. Consequently $S_0(k)=e^{-2ika}\,(K\cos(Ka)+ik\sin(Ka))/(K\cos(Ka)-ik\sin(Ka))$ and $\delta_0=\arg z-ka$ modulo $\pi$, with a nonzero denominator for every positive energy and depth. This is also the actual Wronskian convention of [F1], since outside the well $W(u_0,e^{ikr})=-Bk e^{-i\delta_0}$. Where $\cos(Ka)\ne0$, the equivalent local formula is $\tan(ka+\delta_0)=(k/K)\tan(Ka)$; the complex formula remains valid when either matching value vanishes.

Fix $U>0$ and put $\gamma:=\sqrt{2mU}/\hbar$, so $K=\sqrt{\gamma^2+k^2}$ and $K-\gamma=k^2/(K+\gamma)=O(k^2)$. If $\cos(\gamma a)\ne0$, choose the representative of $\theta$ tending to zero modulo $\pi$. The tangent is smooth near $\gamma a$, so $\tan\theta=(k/K)\tan(Ka)=k\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma+O(k^3)$. By [F2], $\tan\theta=\theta+O(\theta^3)$ near zero; first $\theta=O(k)$ and then $\theta=k\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma+O(k^3)$. Hence $\delta_0=-k a_{\mathrm{eff}}+O(k^3)$ modulo $\pi$, where $a_{\mathrm{eff}}:=a-\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma$, and [F1] gives $\sigma_0\to4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^2$. The expansion uses locally bounded derivatives only where $\cos(\gamma a)\ne0$.

At an exact threshold $\gamma a=\alpha_n:=(n+\tfrac12)\pi$, $n\ge0$, write $s_n:=\sin\alpha_n=(-1)^n$. The identity for $K-\gamma$ and [F2] give $K-\gamma=k^2/(2\gamma)+O(k^4)$, $X=K\cos(Ka)=-s_n a k^2/2+O(k^4)$ and $Y=k\sin(Ka)=s_n k+O(k^5)$. Thus $X/Y=-ak/2+O(k^3)$ and the angle of $X+iY$ tends to $\pi/2$ modulo $\pi$. Writing $\theta=\pi/2+\varepsilon$ modulo $\pi$, $\cot\theta=-\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^3)$ gives $\varepsilon=ak/2+O(k^3)$, so $\delta_0=\pi/2-ak/2+O(k^3)$ modulo $\pi$. Therefore $k^2\sigma_0=4\pi\sin^2\delta_0\to4\pi$; the finite-scattering-length formula of step 3.1 does not apply at this depth. At zero energy the regular reduced solution is proportional to $\sin(\gamma r)$ inside and to the nonzero constant $s_n$ outside, with matching derivative zero at $a$. Its spatial form is proportional to $1/r$ outside and is not square integrable by [F3]; this is the zero-energy s-wave resonance meant here.

In the finite-length branch, as $\gamma a\uparrow\alpha_n$ from below, $\tan(\gamma a)\to+\infty$ and $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to-\infty$; from above $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to+\infty$. Thus the iterated low-energy reading $4\pi a_{\mathrm{eff}}^2$ diverges on either approach, while the exact-threshold law is step 4.1. Along nonresonant depth regimes with $\tan(\gamma a)/\gamma\to0$, $a_{\mathrm{eff}}\to a$ and the iterated low-energy reading tends to $4\pi a^2$, four times the geometric area $\pi a^2$. In particular at $\gamma a=n\pi$, $n\ge1$, $a_{\mathrm{eff}}=a$ and $\delta_0=-ka+O(k^3)$; the interior node tends to the boundary. This comparison holds along the stated depth regimes, rather than for every sequence of large depths.

The bound-state interpretation has a separate negative-energy proof. Write $g:=\gamma a$. For $\alpha_n<g<(n+1)\pi$, define $f_g(x):=x\cot x+\sqrt{g^2-x^2}$ on $[\alpha_n,g]$. It is continuous, $f_g(\alpha_n)=\sqrt{g^2-\alpha_n^2}>0$ and $f_g(g)=g\cot g<0$; [F2] gives a root $x_g\in(\alpha_n,g)$. On that open interval $f_g'=\cot x-x\csc^2x-x/\sqrt{g^2-x^2}<0$, so the root is unique. Put $q:=x_g/a$, $\kappa:=\sqrt{g^2-x_g^2}/a>0$ and $u(r):=\sin(qr)$ for $r\le a$, $u(r):=\sin(qa)e^{-\kappa(r-a)}$ for $r\ge a$. Then $q^2+\kappa^2=\gamma^2$ and $q\cot(qa)=-\kappa$, so both $u$ and $u'$ match at $a$. The spatial function $\psi(x):=u(|x|)/|x|$, with value $q$ at zero, is nonzero and square integrable by [F3]; it is smooth near zero, decays exponentially at infinity and is piecewise smooth with matching first derivatives at $a$. Its weak derivatives through order two are square integrable, with no boundary delta term, hence $\psi\in W^{2,2}$. The radial identity $\Delta(u(r)/r)=u''(r)/r$ for $r>0$ gives $H\psi=-c\kappa^2\psi$, $c=\hbar^2/(2m)$, so normalization produces a genuine s-wave bound eigenvector. As $g\downarrow\alpha_n$, $0<\kappa a\le\sqrt{g^2-\alpha_n^2}\to0$, while for $g\le\alpha_n$ there is no matching root in this branch $x>\alpha_n$ with $x\le g$. Thus a new negative-energy s-wave branch appears just above each stated threshold, whose endpoint is the non-square-integrable zero-energy resonance in step 4.1; no assertion about other angular channels or the full bound-state count is needed.

For the free consistency case $U=0$, $K=k$ and step 2.1 gives $S_0=e^{-2ika}(\cos ka+i\sin ka)/(\cos ka-i\sin ka)=1$, so $\delta_0=0$ modulo $\pi$ at every positive energy, including zeros of sine or cosine. At any positive-depth energy with $Ka=n\pi$, $n\ge1$, one has $Y=0$ and $X\ne0$, hence $S_0=e^{-2ika}$ and $\delta_0=-ka$ modulo $\pi$: this is exactly the exterior phase for the vanishing radial boundary condition of a hard sphere at that energy. If $\cos(Ka)=0$, the same formula gives $S_0=-e^{-2ika}$ and $\delta_0=\pi/2-ka$ modulo $\pi$. These checks complete the full positive-energy, zero-depth and matching-node cases together with the two low-energy branches above.

## Example

**Setup.** Adopt the declared single-channel resonance model
[[def-nrqm-scattering-single-channel-resonance-model]] with channel label
$l=0$, mass $m>0$, action constant $\hbar>0$ and parameters $E_{r}>0$,
$\Gamma>0$; read the phase shift and channel cross section by
[[pthm-nrqm-scattering-single-channel-resonance-cross-section]] clauses (a)-(c).
Put $k_r:=k(E_r)=\hbar^{-1}\sqrt{2mE_r}$ and let $L(E)$ on
$\mathbb R$ denote the auxiliary Lorentzian factor of that theorem.

## Verification

**Given:** the declared model data and the statements of
[[pthm-nrqm-scattering-single-channel-resonance-cross-section]].

1.1 Since $E_r>0$, the theorem can be evaluated at the physical energy $E_r$, giving $\sin^2\delta_0(E_r)=L(E_r)=1$ and $\sigma_0(E_r)=4\pi/k_r^2=4\pi\hbar^2/(2mE_r)$ in $\mathrm{m^2}$. The real-axis factor has $L(E_r\pm\Gamma/2)=1/2$. The upper point is always positive; the lower point is positive exactly if $\Gamma<2E_r$, equals the excluded boundary $0$ if $\Gamma=2E_r$, and is negative if $\Gamma>2E_r$. Only positive points have physical phase and cross-section readings. [given, algebra]

2.1 For every physical $E>0$, with $x:=E-E_r$ and $y:=\Gamma/2>0$, dividing by the positive resonance-centre value yields $\sigma_0(E)/\sigma_0(E_r)=(k_r/k(E))^2 y^2/(x^2+y^2)=(E_r/E)L(E)$. At the always-positive upper point the ratio is $E_r/(2(E_r+y))$; at the lower point it is $E_r/(2(E_r-y))$ only when $E_r-y>0$. If that lower point is zero or negative, the real-axis identity $L(E_r-y)=1/2$ is still valid but no physical ratio is evaluated there. The factor $E_r/E$ is energy dependent and need not vary slowly for arbitrary $\Gamma$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Take the declared parameters $E_{r}=4\,\Gamma$ (both in joules). Then at $E=E_{r}+\Gamma/2=(9/2)\Gamma$ the Lorentzian factor is $1/2$ and the ratio of step 2.1 is $(4/(9/2))(1/2)=4/9$; at $E=(7/2)\Gamma$ the factor is again $1/2$ and the ratio is $(4/(7/2))(1/2)=4/7$. The first value is strictly below $1/2$ and the second strictly above, so this is the explicit asymmetry produced by the $1/E$ factor, so these factor half-height locations are not the locations where $\sigma_0(E)=\sigma_0(E_r)/2$; no maximum of $\sigma_0$ is used in this comparison. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On the full real axis, $L$ reaches $1$ at $E_r$ and $1/2$ exactly at $E_r\pm\Gamma/2$, so its full width at half maximum is $\Gamma$. On the positive physical axis both half-height locations are present exactly when $\Gamma<2E_r$; for $\Gamma\ge2E_r$ the lower location is excluded. This qualifies the physical interpretation without narrowing the allowed $E_r>0$, $\Gamma>0$ parameters or changing the real-axis width identity. The example of step 3.1 keeps both half-height points positive and shows that the cross-section ratios there differ from $1/2$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **No decay claim.** The width parameter $\Gamma$ is an energy parameter of
  the declared factor; the pair does not identify $\hbar/\Gamma$ with a
  lifetime and does not derive an exponential decay law.
- **No maximum claim.** Because of the factor $1/E$ in the ratio computed in
  step 2.1, the pair makes no statement that $\sigma_{0}$ attains its maximum
  at $E_{r}$; only the auxiliary Lorentzian factor's full-real-axis half-height width is asserted, with positive-energy locations qualified above.

derivations.claim: At $E=E_{r}$ the Lorentzian factor of that theorem equals $1$, so $\sin^{2}\delta_{0}(E_{r})=1$ and $\sigma_{0}(E_{r})=4\pi/k_{r}^{2}=4\pi\hbar^{2}/(2mE_{r})$, read in $\mathrm{m^{2}}$; at $E=E_{r}\pm\Gamma/2$ the factor equals $1/2$.

Dividing the general display by the resonance value with $x=E-E_{r}$ and $y=\Gamma/2$ gives $\sigma_{0}(E)/\sigma_{0}(E_{r})=(k_{r}/k(E))^{2}\,y^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})=(E_{r}/E)\,y^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, since $k(E)^{2}\propto E$; at $E=E_{r}\pm\Gamma/2$ this ratio equals $(E_{r}/(E_{r}\pm\Gamma/2))\cdot(1/2)$, which differs from $1/2$ by the slowly varying factor $E_{r}/E$ only.

Take the declared parameters $E_{r}=4\,\Gamma$ (both in joules). Then at $E=E_{r}+\Gamma/2=(9/2)\Gamma$ the Lorentzian factor is $1/2$ and the ratio of step 2.1 is $(4/(9/2))(1/2)=4/9$; at $E=(7/2)\Gamma$ the factor is again $1/2$ and the ratio is $(4/(7/2))(1/2)=4/7$. The first value is strictly below $1/2$ and the second strictly above, so this is the explicit asymmetry produced by the $1/E$ factor, and the half-height points of $\sigma_{0}$ itself are therefore not exactly $E_{r}\pm\Gamma/2$.

By the theorem the factor $\sin^{2}\delta_{0}$ takes the value $1$ at $E_{r}$ and $1/2$ exactly at $E_{r}\pm\Gamma/2$, so its full width at half maximum in energy is $\Gamma$; this is a statement about the declared factor only, not about a measured line shape.

## Example

**Setup.** Adopt the declared short-range scattering model
[[def-nrqm-scattering-framework-short-range-model]] with mass $m>0$, spin
zero, action constant $\hbar>0$ and the **uniform ball potential**
$$V(x):=\begin{cases}V_{0},&|x|<R,\\ 0,&|x|>R,\end{cases}\qquad V_{0}\in\mathbb R,\ R>0,$$
read in joules and metres; adopt the stationary beam model at wave number
$k>0$ and direction $d$, and let $W=(2m/\hbar^{2})V$, $q=\|K_{k}\|$, $f_{k}$
and the Born amplitude $f_{B}$ be as in
[[pthm-nrqm-scattering-controlled-born-approximation]]. Write
$\theta$ for the scattering angle, $\cos\theta=\Omega\cdot d$, and
$q_{\mathrm{tr}}:=|k(d-\Omega)|=2k\sin(\theta/2)$ for the momentum transfer.

## Verification

**Given:** the declared model data, the Born theorem of the pair, and the polar-coordinates formula for Lebesgue measure.

1.1 By the Born theorem, $f_{B}(\Omega)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{B_{R}}e^{iq_{\mathrm{tr}}\cdot y}W(y)\,dy$ with $W=V_{0}2m/\hbar^{2}$ constant on $B_{R}$; in polar coordinates the ball integral is $\int_{B_{R}}e^{iq\cdot y}dy=2\pi\int_{0}^{R}\int_{-1}^{1}e^{iqrs}r^{2}\,ds\,dr=4\pi\bigl(\sin(qR)-qR\cos(qR)\bigr)/q^{3}$ for $q=q_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$, and equals $4\pi R^{3}/3$ at $q=0$ by continuity. [given, algebra]

1.2 The kernel $G_{k}(x-y)W(y)$ on $B_{R}\times B_{R}$ has squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm $\int_{B_{R}}\int_{B_{R}}|G_{k}(x-y)W(y)|^{2}dx\,dy=\frac{|V_{0}|^{2}(2m/\hbar^{2})^{2}}{16\pi^{2}}\int_{B_{R}}\int_{B_{R}}|x-y|^{-2}dx\,dy$; for each $y$ the inner integral over $x\in B_{R}$ is at most the integral over the ball of radius $2R$ around $y$, which is $8\pi R$. Hence $\|K_{k}\|\le\|K_{k}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}R^{2}\sqrt{2/3}=:q_{\mathrm{HS}}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Therefore $f_{B}(\Omega)=-\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\cdot\frac{\sin(q_{\mathrm{tr}}R)-q_{\mathrm{tr}}R\cos(q_{\mathrm{tr}}R)}{q_{\mathrm{tr}}^{3}}$ for $q_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$, with the forward value $f_{B}(\theta=0)=-\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\frac{R^{3}}{3}$; the amplitude has the dimension of length, since $2mV_{0}/\hbar^{2}$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$ and the bracket in $\mathrm{m^{3}}$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Consequently, if $\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}R^{2}\sqrt{2/3}<1$, then $q=\|K_{k}\|\le q_{\mathrm{HS}}<1$ and the controlled Born estimate of the theorem applies; since $t\mapsto t/(1-t)$ is increasing on $[0,1)$ and $\|e_{\mathrm{inc}}\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}=|B_{R}|^{1/2}$, the uniform error bound is at most $|f_{k}(\Omega)-f_{B}(\Omega)|\le\frac{\|W\|_{\infty}|B_{R}|}{4\pi}\frac{q_{\mathrm{HS}}}{1-q_{\mathrm{HS}}}=\frac{2m|V_{0}|}{\hbar^{2}}\frac{R^{3}}{3}\frac{q_{\mathrm{HS}}}{1-q_{\mathrm{HS}}}$ in metres; this is an explicit condition on the declared strength, radius, mass and action constant, verified here without any numerical value of the constants. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Under the same condition the beam model reads $d\sigma/d\Omega(0)=|f_{k}(0)|^{2}$, and the theorem controls the difference from $|f_{B}(0)|^{2}$ through the bound of 2.2; the pair asserts the display $|f_{B}(0)|^{2}=\bigl(\frac{2mV_{0}}{\hbar^{2}}\bigr)^{2}\frac{R^{6}}{9}$ as the Born forward reading, read in $\mathrm{m^{2}\,sr^{-1}}$, and no measured value. [step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Scope.** The Born amplitude is a conditional model quantity; the explicit
  condition of 2.2 is sufficient for the controlled error bound of the pair
  and is not claimed to be necessary.
- **No weak-potential language.** The pair avoids "for a weak potential";
  the condition is the operator-norm condition $q<1$, verified here through
  the displayed Hilbert-Schmidt bound.

**(b) The declared one-centre Coulomb model.** As an additional model
assumption of the pair, fix a real **coupling** $\kappa>0$ with the declared
unit $\mathrm{J\,m}$ and put
$$\gamma:=\frac{2m\kappa}{\hbar^{2}}\qquad(\text{unit }\mathrm{m^{-1}}),\qquad C_{\gamma}:=-\Delta-\frac{\gamma}{|\cdot|}\ \text{ on }\ D(C_{\gamma})=H^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C),$$

energy operator** of the one-centre Coulomb model is
$$H_{\kappa}:=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,C_{\gamma},$$
with domain $D(H_{\kappa}):=D(C_{\gamma})$; by
[[lem-nrqm-potentials-positive-scaling-of-self-adjoint-operators]] clauses (a)
and (b) it is self-adjoint with the same domain, and by
[[lem-nrqm-central-free-operator-differential-identification]] together with
the action formula of the cited theorem it acts by
$$H_{\kappa}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f-\kappa\frac{f}{|\cdot|}\qquad(f\in D(H_{\kappa})),$$
where $\Delta_{w}$ is the weak Laplacian. The model declares the **length
scale** $a_{\kappa}:=\hbar^{2}/(m\kappa)$, read in metres, and the **energy
scale** $\mathcal E_{\kappa}:=m\kappa^{2}/(2\hbar^{2})=\hbar^{2}/(2ma_{\kappa}^{2})$,
read in joules. The model adopts $(H_{\kappa},\mathrm J)$ as its declared
energy observable for the one-centre problem; the self-adjointness is the
cited theorem's and no spectral property is presupposed here.

$(A_{l})_{l\ge0}$ be the unitary and the radial operators of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] clauses (a)-(d):
$U$ maps $H_{0}$ onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^{2}((0,\infty),dr;\mathbb C)$ with
$UH_{\kappa}U^{*}=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}(\hbar^{2}/2m)A_{l}$, and each $A_{l}$ is self-adjoint
with form domain $V_{l}$ and domain $D(A_{l})$. The model declares the
**sector $(l,m)$ radial energy operator** $A_{l}^{(\kappa)}:=(\hbar^{2}/2m)A_{l}$,
read in joules, and, for a class $u\in D(A_{l})$, the **declared radial
equation** is the distributional identity
$$-u''(r)+\Bigl(\frac{l(l+1)}{r^{2}}-\frac{\gamma}{r}\Bigr)u(r)=A_{l}u(r)\qquad\text{on }(0,\infty),$$
which by clause (c) of the cited theorem is an ordinary differential equation
with $C^{2}$ representative whenever $A_{l}u=Eu$ for a constant $E$. The
**regular reduced solution** at energy attribute $k>0$ is the function
$u_{\mathrm{reg}}(r)=r^{l+1}e^{-kr}v(2kr)$ of clause (c) of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]], with $v$ the regular

theorems of the page identify it.

take two **distinguishable** spinless massive particles with declared mass

$$\kappa:=\frac{q^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}},\qquad \varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1},$$

$c$ the speed of light, both as in clause (c) of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; the identification $\kappa=q^{2}/(4\pi\varepsilon_{0})$

two copies of the one-particle space of clause (a) as in
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], identified with
$L^{2}(\mathbb R^{6};\mathbb C)$ through
[[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]]; the spin-zero internal
factor is trivial, and because the two particles are of different species no
symmetrisation is imposed (the case of identical species belongs to the
identical-particle sector of P6 and is not used here). The **assigned energy
operator** is
$$H_{2}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{1}}\Delta_{x_{1}}-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{2}}\Delta_{x_{2}}-\frac{\kappa}{|x_{1}-x_{2}|},\qquad D(H_{2}):=H^{2}(\mathbb R^{6};\mathbb C),$$
which is self-adjoint by clause (c) of

unitary $U_{\Phi}$. The model declares the **centre-of-mass/relative reading**

and the **relative operator** $C_{\mu}:=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2\mu}\Delta_{r}-\frac{\kappa}{|r|}$;

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

**(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about sharp and unsharp real-valued quantities. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The latter is the explicit hypothesis used to obtain the spectral PVM of a general self-adjoint operator from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] in clause (ii); consumers invoking this construction inherit it.

**(i) Sharp observables.** An **ideal sharp real-valued quantity** (observable) of a system with state space $H$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), together with a declared unit in which its real spectral coordinate is read; the unit is part of the assignment, and no numerical value of the coordinate is asserted by the assignment. Symmetry of $A$ on a small domain is not sufficient for self-adjointness, and the domain is a declared part of the observable.

**(ii) Spectral probability.** Let $E_{A}$ be the spectral projection-valued measure of the self-adjoint operator $A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ the **probability of the outcome in $B$** is
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{A}(B)\bigr),\qquad\text{and for a pure preparation }[\psi]\text{ it is }\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_{A}(B)\psi\|^{2}.$$
By clause (b) of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] the assignment $B\mapsto\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets ([[def-probability-measure]], [[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). It is the general form of the Born rule adopted here.

**(iii) Nature of the outcome law.** The probability law is a measure, not necessarily a density with respect to Lebesgue measure and not necessarily a finite or countable sum of point masses: a self-adjoint operator with continuous spectrum ordinarily has no normalizable eigenvector at a point of its continuous spectrum, so an "exact value" of a continuum quantity is not represented by a normalized state. An ideal point value is an idealization; a real detector reports a finite-resolution outcome, that is, the probability of a declared Borel set $B$ such as a bin, and the recorded-event probability is that of (ii) for the bin, not the value of a density at a point.

**(iv) Unsharp finite outcomes.** Outcomes of a finite-resolution apparatus with finitely many channels are described, when the idealization uses bounded effects, by a finite family $(F_{a})_{a=1}^{p}$ of bounded operators with $0\le F_{a}\le I$ in the quadratic-form order and $\sum_{a}F_{a}=I$ ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (a)), the **outcome probabilities** being $p_{a}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})\ge0$, $\sum_{a}p_{a}=1$ by clause (b) of the same lemma. This unsharp extension is an operational description tied to an apparatus model; it is not obtained from the sharp observable by mathematical manipulation alone, and the effects alone do not determine what happens to the state after the outcome (P3).

**(v) Moments are a separate matter.** Statements about the mean, variance or higher moments of the outcome law require the corresponding integrability of $t\mapsto t^{n}$ against $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ and are not part of this postulate; where they are used they are stated with their hypotheses. In particular the existence of $\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)$ for an unbounded $A$ is not asserted.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model. They assert nothing about which quantities of a concrete apparatus are sharp, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome or about the completeness of the description; a laboratory record is a classical event whose relation to the model is a tested identification with uncertainty, in the sense of P7.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following discipline for comparing the model with recorded data.

**(i) Declared model of each comparison.** A comparison of a model prediction with an experiment of the framework requires, in addition to the state and dynamics assumptions P1-P5, the following declared items: a **preparation model**, that is, a specification of the state or preparation assigned to the system together with the physical procedure that realizes it; an **isolation model**, that is, the energy operator used and a statement of the interactions neglected in the approximation; a **detection model**, that is, the response of the apparatus, including efficiency, resolution, background and any binning; and **sampling assumptions**, that is, the statistical model under which repetitions of the preparation and detection are combined. None of these items is supplied by the mathematical framework alone.

**(ii) Repetitions.** The treatment of repeated trials as independent and identically distributed draws from the model's outcome law is an additional statistical model of the apparatus and the procedure. It is not a consequence of the state postulate and is not guaranteed by the mathematics; where it is assumed it is stated, and where it fails (correlated trials, drifting preparation, dead time, selection) the statistical analysis must model the departure or record the limitation.

**(iii) Identification with uncertainty.** The claim "this apparatus realizes the preparation $\rho$ and the dynamics $H_{\mathrm{op}}$" and the claim "this detector realizes the effect $F$" are physical identifications: they are tested against recorded behaviour of the apparatus, carry uncertainty and can fail. They are not derived from the framework, and a model prediction obtained under them inherits their qualifications. Calibration procedures, control experiments and their limitations are recorded with the comparison.

**(iv) Empirical premises.** Where a measured value enters a deduction - a mass, a charge, a field strength, a detector efficiency - it enters as a qualified empirical premise with its uncertainty, conditions of measurement and source, and the conclusion of the deduction carries those qualifications. A deduction that uses a measured input is not an exact statement about nature.

**(v) Status.** Clauses (i)-(iv) are adopted as the framework's conditions for comparing model with data. They make no claim that the framework or the apparatus description is exact; agreement of a prediction with a dataset is evidence about the combined model and apparatus assumptions, not a proof of the framework and not a statement about nature deduced from the mathematics.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Z^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$; the vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is experimentally determined and $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$. These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: $j$ has dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$; it is a probability flux, not a charge flux.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

**(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). **(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. $$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

$$H_{0}:=\mathcal F_{2}^{*}M_{c|\xi|^{2}}\mathcal F_{2},\qquad D(H_{0}):=\bigl\{f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C):|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal F_{2}$ is the unitary Plancherel transform of that theorem.
Let $D^{2}_{j}$ denote the second weak partial derivative in the $j$-th
coordinate, defined componentwise on the locally integrable classes of
$\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]),
write $\Delta_{w}:=D^{2}_{1}+D^{2}_{2}+D^{2}_{3}$ for the weak Laplacian
(defined on the classes whose three second weak partial derivatives lie in
$L^{2}$), and let $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Then:

(a) $D(H_{0})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ as sets and
$$H_{0}f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\,\Delta_{w}f\qquad\text{for every }f\in D(H_{0});$$
equivalently, $\mathcal F_{2}(H_{0}f)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$ and
$\mathcal F_{2}\bigl(-\tfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f\bigr)(\xi)=c|\xi|^{2}\mathcal F_{2}f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$, and the two $L^{2}$ classes agree.

(b) For every real bounded measurable $V:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb R$, the
operator $H_{0}+M_{V}$ of clause (c) of the cited theorem, with domain
$D(H_{0})$, coincides with the operator $f\mapsto-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}f+Vf$
on the same domain; in particular, for $E\in\mathbb R$ and
$\psi\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ the eigenvalue equation
$(H_{0}+M_{V})\psi=E\psi$ is equivalent to the weak equation
$-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{w}\psi+V\psi=E\psi$ elementwise in
